name: ratatouille
instructions:
TWO VARIANTS on the french provincial vegetable-and-tomato dish. Same cornerstone (ONION + TOMATO + BELL PEPPER); different CUT.

- VARIANT A — PROVINCIAL / LATHERA-STYLE: cornerstone vegetables cut very coarse — they're the 'meat' of the dish. Slow-braised in a lot of olive oil (see LATHERA + OIL note). Rustic and chunky.
- VARIANT B — CONFIT BYALDI (KELLER / PIXAR): cornerstone vegetables pureed smooth into a PIPERADE base. Fennel bulb added to the sauce. Paper-thin tianed eggplant + zucchini on top, baked covered then uncovered.

Both served over STEAMED WHITE RICE — non-negotiable (see RICE note).

=== INGREDIENTS (BOTH VARIANTS, WITH VARIANT-SPECIFIC CUTS) ===

CORNERSTONE (onion + tomato + bell pepper — the whole dish rests on these):
- 1 large ONION — coarse chunks / thick rings in variant A; chopped and pureed in variant B
- 2-3 ripe TOMATOES (or canned for variant B) — coarse chop in A; pureed in B
- 2 BELL PEPPERS (green preferred — Julia Child's call) — thick rings or coarse chunks in A; chopped and pureed in B

ALSO IN THE SAUCE / BASE:
- 1-2 CARROTS — very finely diced (or pureed) in variant A; pureed as part of the piperade in variant B. Always in.
- 4-6 cloves GARLIC (primary — see note; Julia canonical, I'd skip it if it were up to me)
- 1 fennel bulb, coarse chunks (VARIANT B specifically — in the piperade sauce)
- Fennel powder + herbes de provence (see SEASONINGS note — always a winner)
- Salt + black pepper
- Generous OLIVE OIL throughout (LOTS in variant A per lathera)

TIAN / TOP-LAYER VEGETABLES (both variants):
- 1 ZUCCHINI, sliced into rounds — thick in variant A / thin for the tian
- 1 EGGPLANT, sliced into rounds — thick in variant A / thin for the tian
- (Optional) 1 summer squash, sliced similarly

SERVING:
- Steamed WHITE RICE (see RICE note — non-negotiable)

=== VARIANT A — PROVINCIAL / LATHERA-STYLE PROCEDURE ===

1. In a heavy pan with a GENEROUS amount of olive oil, add coarse-chopped onion (thick rings), bell peppers (thick rings), garlic, and the finely-diced carrot. Sauté briefly to soften.
2. Add coarsely-chopped fresh tomatoes. Season with fennel powder, herbes de provence, salt, and black pepper.
3. Simmer covered on low heat 20-30 min until silky and starting to break down — lathera register.
4. For the zucchini and eggplant, use the EGGPLANT + ZUCCHINI TECHNIQUE note. Both approaches work here.
5. Serve over steamed white rice.

=== VARIANT B — CONFIT BYALDI / PIPERADE PROCEDURE ===

1. Sauté chopped onion, bell peppers, chopped fennel bulb, garlic, and finely-chopped carrot in olive oil until soft. Add tomatoes (canned or fresh). Simmer 20-30 min.
2. PUREE SMOOTH (immersion blender in the pan, or transfer to a blender). Season with fennel powder, herbes de provence, salt, black pepper.
3. Spread the smooth piperade evenly across a shallow oven-safe dish.
4. Slice zucchini and eggplant very thinly (mandoline). Arrange in overlapping rings or rows on top of the piperade.
5. See EGGPLANT + ZUCCHINI TECHNIQUE note for the bake.
6. Serve over steamed white rice.
notes:
=== VARIANT A IS A LATHERA — NEEDS LOTS OF OIL ===

Variant A borrows the greek LATHERA technique (coarse vegetable braise in generous olive oil). Lots of oil is load-bearing here — it's the medium the vegetables braise in, and reducing it makes the dish read dry and flat. This is closer to fasolakia-lathera or rustic italian caponata than to a plated ratatouille. Don't skimp on the olive oil.

=== CORNERSTONE VEGETABLES — ONION + TOMATO + BELL PEPPER ARE THE MEAT ===

The onion + tomato + bell pepper trio is the whole dish. In variant A they're the visible chunky components — cut them as coarsely as possible (thick rings for onion + peppers, coarse chop for tomato) and let them keep their identity through the braise. In variant B they get pureed smooth into the piperade base.

CARROTS ALWAYS IN — FINE OR PUREED: 1-2 carrots go in either variant. Very finely diced for variant A (should disappear into the tomato base rather than sit as visible orange bits), pureed as part of the piperade for variant B.

FENNEL BULB IS VARIANT B ONLY: chopped fennel bulb goes into the piperade base for variant B. Not part of variant A's cornerstone chunks.

=== SEASONINGS — FENNEL POWDER + HERBES DE PROVENCE (ALWAYS A WINNER) ===

Fennel powder + herbes de provence is the seasoning combo that always works here. Both variants take the same seasoning. Salt and black pepper obviously; fennel seeds crushed in a mortar are welcome alongside the powder.

=== WHITE WINE — TESTED, JUST UNNECESSARY ===

White wine sounds tempting here (a splash for acid + wine character in the tomato base). I've tried it. It really doesn't need it — the dish just doesn't need wine, period. Even when the wine seems to add something, it's because you added VERY LITTLE (less than 1/4 cup) — at that quantity anything is neutral-to-mildly-positive. But the version without wine is what actually reads correct.

Not clashing per se — the dish doesn't fall apart with wine. Just unnecessary. Save the wine for something that actually benefits from it (a stew or braise where wine is doing structural work), not this.

=== HAZARDS — WHAT TO WATCH FOR ===

Three ways this dish goes wrong that are worth calling out up front:

1. OVERDOING PARSLEY OR CARROTS — MAKES IT SWEETER THAN IT SHOULD BE: parsley and carrots are NON-NATIVES to the tomato/onion/bell pepper cornerstone. Each has a role (small amount of parsley for finish if you want it; 1-2 carrots for base sweetness), but both are easy to overdo. When overdone, the whole dish reads SWEETER than it should. Keep parsley restrained (or skip like I do); don't add extra carrots beyond the 1-2 in the base. (White wine used to be in this hazard list — walked back further; see WHITE WINE note below — just omit it entirely.)

2. JULIA CHILD'S SALTING METHOD CAN BACKFIRE — BRINEY VEGETABLES: Julia recommends salting eggplant (and sometimes zucchini) heavily to draw out bitter water. Done wrong, you end up with BRINEY vegetables that carry too much salt into the finished dish. I USUALLY SKIP the salt-and-drain step entirely. See SALT LIGHTLY note below for the fuller rule.

3. SAUTÉING ZUCCHINI IS HAZARDOUS (IF YOU GO THAT ROUTE): pan too hot OR too much oil = WET, SOGGY, DESTROYED zucchini drowned in oil. If sautéing (per Julia's separate-cooking approach), keep the pan temperature MODERATE (not too hot) and use a RESTRAINED amount of oil (not enough to drown the strips). Both mistakes send the zucchini into mush-and-oil territory that can't be walked back. The tian-on-top approach (see EGGPLANT + ZUCCHINI TECHNIQUE) sidesteps this hazard entirely.

=== GARLIC — PRIMARY, JULIA CHILD CANONICAL (I'D SKIP IT) ===

Garlic is primary here because Julia Child specifies it in her ratatouille. Left to my own preference I'd skip it — the dish doesn't need it structurally — but it's canonical enough that primary is right. If you want to lean my preference, 1-2 cloves instead of 4-6 keeps garlic present but not assertive.

=== PARSLEY (SECONDARY) — JULIA CANONICAL BUT I SKIP IT ===

Parsley is another Julia canonical add that I typically skip. Kept in secondary — welcome as a fresh finish if you want it; not on the standard ingredient list.

=== EGGPLANT + ZUCCHINI TECHNIQUE — TWO APPROACHES ===

JULIA CHILD'S APPROACH (BEST, TIME-CONSUMING): prepare the zucchini and eggplant SEPARATELY from the tomato-vegetable base.
- ZUCCHINI: sauté in the pan, remove, and set aside BEFORE making the stew/piperade base. Freed pan is then used for the base.
- EGGPLANT: roast in the oven while you're making the stew/piperade on the stovetop. Saves time via parallel cooking.
- Combine everything at the end.
This is the technique that produces the best result. It's also genuinely time-consuming — two extra cook streams alongside the main base.

MY SIMPLER APPROACH (WORKS FOR BOTH VARIANTS): slice zucchini and eggplant, arrange on TOP of whatever the base is (blended piperade for variant B, chunky lathera stew for variant A). Bake COVERED at ~275-300°F, then UNCOVERED at 400°F to lightly color the tops. Faster; requires less pan juggling; still delivers a proper ratatouille.

Either approach is fine. Pick by how much time you have.

=== SERVE WITH STEAMED WHITE RICE — NON-NEGOTIABLE ===

This dish should ALWAYS go with steamed white rice. I find it inedible without the rice — the olive-oil-and-tomato base needs a starch to sit on that catches and holds the sauce. Bread doesn't work here (soaks up the sauce wrong); rice does. Both variants read well over white rice, including variant B (fine-dining plating traditionally goes without rice; I still put it on rice at home).

=== SALT LIGHTLY — DON'T PRE-SALT / BRINE THE EGGPLANT + ZUCCHINI ===

Common technique advice is to salt eggplant heavily to draw out bitter water. In this recipe that advice is a trap — the vegetables end up carrying salt into a base that's already seasoned, and the finished dish reads over-salted with no walk-back. Err on the side of too little salt on the vegetables. Season the tomato base incrementally as you build it.

=== DON'T OVERDO THE TOMATO ===

The tomato element seasons and adorns the vegetables (variant A) or forms the base bed under them (variant B) — it's not the main event either way. Overloading with tomato swamps the vegetable character. Modest quantities; if the sauce feels thin, reduce further rather than adding more.

=== BELL PEPPER CHOICE — GREEN OVER RED/YELLOW/ORANGE (JULIA'S CALL) ===

Green bell pepper's more vegetal / grassy character holds up against the tomato better than the sweetness of the colored varieties. Julia was explicit on this point.

=== RED CHILI FLAKES (SECONDARY) — A LITTLE HEAT IS NICE ===

A pinch of red chili flakes stirred into the base is a nice add — a background heat that lifts the tomato-and-vegetable register. Not classical (Julia doesn't call for it); secondary. Small pinch, not enough to make the dish read spicy.

=== SUMMER SQUASH (SECONDARY) — NOT MY FAVORITE ADDITION ===

Summer squash (yellow crookneck or similar) is a common addition alongside the zucchini + eggplant, and it does fill in a third color / texture register. Secondary here because I'm not really into it — the zucchini + eggplant combination is enough. Include if you like it and want more variety; skip otherwise.

=== NO VINEGAR ===

Don't add red wine vinegar, balsamic, or any acid beyond what tomatoes bring (and the small splash of white wine). Ratatouille sits in an olive-oil-and-tomato register that vinegar pushes toward italian caponata territory (a different, more sour-sweet dish).

=== OPTIONAL — CORN-FRIED ZUCCHINI SLICES ON TOP ===

Instead of sautéed / tianed zucchini rounds, swap in corn-fried-zucchini-slices — thin zucchini rounds dredged in a milk-and-egg wash then masa harina, pan-fried until crisp. Adds a distinct crunchy / corn-crusted textural element on top of the tomato-vegetable base. Works best served immediately (the corn crust softens as it cools).
original_chef: Classical french provincial dish. Variant A is my lathera-adjacent adaptation; Variant B is Thomas Keller's confit byaldi (via the Pixar movie). Cornerstone ingredients (garlic, parsley, green bell pepper) per Julia Child's version.
